SRS11-P1-1.solved: Final paragraph settles it: "What she had undertaken was not to decide whether the letters should arrive. It was to wait until she was asked a second time" — and para 3 says he "had not asked again." The promise, unreleased.
SRS11-P1-1.note: C, D and E are each the villagers' theories from para 2, which para 3 explicitly discounts ("None of the three had been in the sorting room"). That is a well-built option set. B is defeated by the same closing lines — she can account for it.

SRS11-P1-2.solved: Para 1: "In January she took it out again and put it in a tin ... on the shelf above the stove." The drawer under the scales (C) is the intermediate step, not the eventual one; "eventually" in the stem is doing the work.
SRS11-P1-2.note: C is the one real trap and it is a fair one. E (burned in the stove) borrows 'stove' from the key's own sentence; D and B are unsupported.

SRS11-P1-3.solved: The clause that follows the quoted phrase is the whole answer: "a strange, lawyerly way of speaking for a man she had never heard use a word of more than two syllables." The oddity is the mismatch between the request and the man.
SRS11-P1-3.note: E (he had learned the words beforehand) is the nearest miss and is the kind of thing a strong reader might build, but nothing on the page supports rehearsal; the text gives the contrast explicitly, so C wins on the sentence as written. A is refuted — she understood well enough to comply for 31 years.

SRS11-P1-4.solved: Para 3 opens "None of the three had been in the sorting room on the morning Bryn Cadoc came in" and then narrates what Ottilie herself saw and remembered thinking. Para 2 was three people who were not there.
SRS11-P1-4.note: A is close in shape but the narrator shows no distrust of Ottilie; the distrust in para 2 attaches to the schoolmaster, 'fond of a grievance'. Good organization item.

SRS11-P1-5.solved: "Thirty-one Decembers is a long while ... Ottilie had had leisure to consider that the promise had been a foolish one" — the paragraph is measuring elapsed time, so 'leisure' = ample time.
SRS11-P1-5.note: B (ease of mind) is the intended trap and is well chosen — the sentence is about brooding, so the wrong sense feels right until you notice the paragraph's opening clause is about duration. C and D are the everyday senses. Clean SSAT vocab-in-context.

SRS11-P2-1.solved: Para 2 defines the instrument ("a cast made from a mould taken off another cast is smaller again"); para 3 finds 61 sitting "a further step down". That is a second-generation group.
SRS11-P2-1.note: See cross-item note on SRS11-P2-3: this key and that one are the same fact in two wordings.

SRS11-P2-2.solved: Para 3: "Every one of them had been bought between 1919 and 1923, and no cast bought in those five years fell into the other group."
SRS11-P2-2.note: A, B and D name attributes the passage never mentions at all — a student cannot produce them from any wrong path through the text. E is the only one with a hook (the marbles of para 1) and it is the only distractor earning its place.

SRS11-P2-3.solved: Para 4: moulding shop flooded and "out of use for four years", yet the 1920 catalogue is "the largest it ever issued" — "A workshop that is selling more heads than it can mould must be getting them from somewhere."
SRS11-P2-3.note: B overreaches on 'for good' — the passage says four years. D and E are the invented-cause family. Strongest item of the set on its own; weakest on independence (see leakage).

SRS11-P2-4.solved: "The complaint was minuted, thanked, and not acted upon ... it is the only contemporary notice of a difference that anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers at any time in the seventy years that followed. Vass says so twice." The last four words are the tone marker.
SRS11-P2-4.note: B is a genuine trap because para 4 does say the Institute 'could not have known' about Bramm's flooding — but para 5 is about what it could have measured and didn't. The paragraph restriction in the stem is load-bearing and correctly placed.
SRS11-P2-4.hedge_option: A — 'unwilling to say whether anybody was at fault'

SRS11-P2-5.solved: "they answer to one another closely but not to the rest" — the 61 measurements match each other. 'Correspond to'.
SRS11-P2-5.note: C (reply to) is the everyday sense and the right trap; D (be responsible to) is the second-commonest idiom ('answer to a supervisor') and also fair.

SRS11-P3-1.solved: The record advances 19 days over 22 years (para 1); para 3 attributes 11 of the 19 to doubled walking effort; para 4 rules the clearance out; para 5 concedes warming but refuses to let the figure carry it. No single cause survives.
SRS11-P3-1.note: A, B, C and E are all counterfactual inventions rather than misreadings — none has a foothold in the text, so the item collapses to 'did you notice the passage is about confounds'. That is also why it leaks into P3-3 and P3-4.
SRS11-P3-1.hedge_option: D — 'cannot be put down to one cause' is the unresolved/declines-to-adjudicate option

SRS11-P3-2.solved: Para 3, first sentence: "In 2004 she began walking the heath weekly instead of fortnightly."
SRS11-P3-2.note: B and D are contradicted elsewhere in the passage ('The route did not change'), A and C are pure inventions. Pure lookup.

SRS11-P3-3.solved: Para 4: if clearance were the driver the two cleared banks "should have run ahead of the other three from 1999 onward. They did not." Cleared and uncleared advance together.
SRS11-P3-3.note: A is the exact inversion of the finding and is the right trap. This is close to a detail item wearing an inference label — the paragraph states the negative result outright.
SRS11-P3-3.hedge_option: E — 'did not by itself' is a hedged/qualified formulation (borderline); it is the key

SRS11-P3-4.solved: Para 5: the figure "has now appeared twice in print as evidence of a warming climate ... and she has written to both. Her record cannot be evidence of that." Writing to both publications is the annoyance.
SRS11-P3-4.note: A is the well-made trap: she does decline to say what the 19 days mean causally, but she is entirely definite about the USE, which is what the stem asks. 'Irritation' is a mild intensification of 'disputes ... has written to both' — supported, but it is the one word in this key I would call an inference rather than a paraphrase.
SRS11-P3-4.hedge_option: A — 'reluctance to say whether the figure means anything at all'

SRS11-P3-5.solved: "a record of this kind ... is only as sound as the walking behind it" — the record's trustworthiness depends on the fieldwork. 'Reliable'.
SRS11-P3-5.note: A (sensible) is the strong trap since 'sound reasoning' is the commonest figurative sense; but a record is not sensible or otherwise, and 'as sound as the walking behind it' is a dependence claim. B (unbroken) is a decent second trap for a time series. Well built.

SRS11-P4-1.solved: The last paragraph reverses the apparent stance: "It was not modesty ... He was right and I was wrong, and the argument took ten minutes, which was nine more than it should have." The piece is about regretting her own refusal.
SRS11-P4-1.note: C is the trap the first four paragraphs set up and the final paragraph demolishes; a student who stops reading at para 4 picks C. E is refuted (he offered the credit; she declined). This is the best-constructed item in the batch. Minor wording snag: 'a refusal she made herself' can be parsed as 'a refusal she forced herself into' — both parses land on the same item, but 'her own refusal' would be cleaner.
SRS11-P4-1.hedge_option: A — 'uncertainty about what passed between them that winter'

SRS11-P4-2.solved: Para 2: "He did not pay me in money. He paid me in books ... I could have the duplicates from his own shelves instead."
SRS11-P4-2.note: D (thirty pounds) is the good trap — the figure is in the paragraph, but it is the scholar's whole budget for the edition, not her fee. A is defeated by the books themselves.

SRS11-P4-3.solved: Para 3: "He had not asked me first. He said it as a thing already decided, which was the way he said most things." He assumed she would want it.
SRS11-P4-3.note: A (making up for having paid her so little) is the option I want to flag: it is exactly the inference a competent student invents from para 2, and the passage gives it no textual hook whatsoever. It does not defeat D — D is stated — but it is the item's real risk. C is refuted by 'He argued for about ten minutes'.

SRS11-P4-4.solved: Para 5: "It was not modesty. It was that I did not want to be found out later in a claim I could not defend, and that is a thing you do for yourself and not for the book" + "nine more [minutes] than it should have".
SRS11-P4-4.note: A is explicitly negated by the text ('It was not modesty') — a sharp distractor. C ('could not have known better') is the sympathetic reading the last paragraph withholds. Strong item in isolation; see leakage with P4-1.
SRS11-P4-4.hedge_option: B — 'still unsure whether the refusal was the right one'

SRS11-P4-5.solved: "He was plain with me about it. He wrote that he had thirty pounds ... that thirty pounds would not buy four hundred and eleven letters from anybody" — he told her the awkward truth. 'Candid'.
SRS11-P4-5.note: A, C, D and E are the four other live senses of 'plain' and all are idiomatic English, which is what a good vocabulary-in-context option set looks like. The 'plain with me' collocation makes B unambiguous.

SRS11-P5-1.solved: Opening: "when the lettering on a village war memorial goes shallow, the parish should leave it shallow"; close: "The wear is the one part of a memorial that cannot be commissioned."
SRS11-P5-1.note: B is the position the essay is written against; C, D and E are compromise positions the essay never entertains. Fine main-idea item, but it makes P5-5 and most of P5-4 free.

SRS11-P5-2.solved: Para 2: the roll was "cut again ... a good deal deeper than the original", and the consequence he objects to follows immediately — "Ninety years of weather came off that stone in three days."
SRS11-P5-2.note: THIS IS THE ITEM I HAD TO REACH ON. A is the only option the passage asserts about Chaldon, so it wins by elimination — but it misnames the objection. The writer does not object to the depth; he objects to re-cutting at all (he praises the mason's work, and para 3 shows the re-cutting was unnecessary because every name could still be read). 'The names could all still be read' is the objection and is not on the list. E is not defensible — he never says the money had a better use, he says it bought a loss — but a careful student who notices A misdescribes the argument has nowhere good to go. Recommend rewriting the key toward the removal of the wear, or adding the readability option.

SRS11-P5-3.solved: Para 3 opens "I will allow one exception and it is narrower than it sounds", states the exception (a name gone entirely), then narrows it: "That is not a licence to re-cut the memorial. It is a licence to re-cut a name."
SRS11-P5-3.note: A describes paragraph FOUR ('They are tidy people ... Nobody has ever asked them to examine the wish'), which makes it a precise near-miss keyed to the adjacent paragraph — the best distractor in the batch.
SRS11-P5-3.hedge_option: B — concede-then-qualify shape; it is the key

SRS11-P5-4.solved: Para 4: "I do not think the parishes that do this are careless of their memorials. They are the opposite. They are tidy people" — combined with the whole essay's verdict that the practice destroys the memorial.
SRS11-P5-4.note: E is directly negated by the paragraph's first sentence, which is the right way to build a tone distractor. B is the true hedge and is correctly not the key — but the key C is itself a both-sides-shaped option ('both that they mean well and that they are wrong'), so this item counts on both sides of the hedging tally depending on how strictly 'hedged' is defined. It is not a refusal to adjudicate: he adjudicates.
SRS11-P5-4.hedge_option: B — 'unable to decide whether their reasons are good ones' (not key); C is both-sides-shaped and IS the key

SRS11-P5-5.solved: "But the memorial's office is not to be legible" — what the stone is FOR. 'Proper function'. Echoed by para 3, "the stone has stopped doing the one thing it was put up to do".
SRS11-P5-5.note: A genuinely archaic sense, well cued by context, with A (a religious service) a real competing sense in a war-memorial setting and E (a position of authority) live too. Best vocabulary item of the six. Slightly above SSAT Upper Level median difficulty but legitimately gettable from context.

SRS11-P6-1.solved: Para 4: dairy vs. flax retting-and-drying, "both trades wanted cool and dark", nothing diagnostic came out of the 1974 lift, "I could not tell you which it was, and I know of nothing short of a new excavation that would."
SRS11-P6-1.note: B is the sharp trap — the 1974 lift is real and settled nothing. D and E are counterfactual. See leakage: this key is recoverable from P6-5 and vice versa.
SRS11-P6-1.hedge_option: C — 'has not been settled'; it is the key

SRS11-P6-2.solved: Para 3: "It is flagged; the flags are laid to a fall of about an inch in seven feet; and at the low corner there is a drain." Also 'a flagged floor' in para 1.
SRS11-P6-2.note: A, B, C and D are four floor types with no presence in the passage — no wrong path through the text produces any of them. Pure recall; acceptable as the easy item of the set but the option shell is doing nothing.

SRS11-P6-3.solved: Para 2: "the jambs carry the sockets for a bar — on the passage side. A room barred from outside is a room for keeping things in." The writer draws the conclusion himself in the next sentence.
SRS11-P6-3.note: C and D are the archaeology-flavoured wrong turns and are fair; the passage says the jambs are 'original', which kills both. The stem's 'chiefly in order to' is answered literally by the following sentence, so this is easier than a purpose item usually is.

SRS11-P6-4.solved: Last paragraph: "the vault is bonded into the outer wall, course for course, and went up when the house went up ... it was wanted from the first."
SRS11-P6-4.note: Labelled 'inference' but it is a one-step paraphrase of an explicit sentence — 'went up when the house went up' IS 'belonged to the original plan'. A, D and E are each a clean negation of the bonding evidence, which makes them good options attached to a soft stem. Consider re-labelling as detail, or moving the evidence a paragraph away from the question.

SRS11-P6-5.solved: Para 2 dismantles the story on three counts — bar sockets on the outside, no inside bar ever, an unglazed unshuttered window at standing-man height over the yard — and the writer says "The window settles what is left of the story." Para 1's aside that it entered the 1888 county volume "without a question mark" is the antiquity-is-no-warrant note.
SRS11-P6-5.note: Mild reach on the key's second clause: 'untroubled by how old it is' has to be built from the 1888 aside and 'for as long as anyone has been asking' — supported, but by implication rather than statement, and a student could hesitate over it. D is the real trap because para 4 DOES hedge ('Here the case stops, and I want to be honest about where') — but it hedges between the two trades, not about the Herrons. That distinction is the item, and it is a good one.
SRS11-P6-5.hedge_option: D — 'unwilling to say whether it is true'
